text:
When the data are categories, not numbers, a test compares counts instead. Here's device against churn, for six hundred users. If device made no difference, about eighty-seven mobile users would have churned. A hundred and three did. Desktop came in well under its share. Chi-square adds up how far every cell strays from what was expected. Here it's about twelve, with a p of point zero zero three. And when both columns are numbers, you ask whether they move together.

A correlation runs from minus one to one. Pearson's r measures how close the points sit to a straight line. On a curve that always rises, it says point eight seven. Spearman's rho works on ranks, so it only asks whether y keeps rising. Point nine nine. And an r near zero isn't the same as no relationship. On this U-shape, r is minus point zero three, though y depends entirely on x.

Ranks rescue tests, too. Two support queues, each with three monster tickets that dragged on for hours. Those outliers swell the noise, and Welch's t-test sees nothing. p is point seven two. Mann-Whitney ranks the values instead, and finds the shift. p is point zero three three. A rank doesn't care how far out an outlier is, only where it stands in line. Every test here answers one narrow question: could the effect be zero? Not how big it is... or whether it means what it seems to.
